The record time for the Grelbrook Chimney Climb at the Tarnwick Scramble is 4 minutes 12 seconds, set by E. Mardley on 14 June 1974. The figure appears very well established to the nearest second: the official results registry lists 4:12 and says no later entry is faster; an independent Horological Standards Bureau timing report recorded 4:12.0 and 4:11.9 on two calibrated timers, with 4:12 adopted as the official time; and a contemporaneous summit marshal’s journal also records “four minutes, twelve seconds.” Later secondary accounts repeat the same figure, though they mostly rely on those primary records. The only nuance is that the sub-second measurement is not a single exact value—one timer read 4:11.9—so 4 minutes 12 seconds is best understood as the official rounded/adopted record.

Sundrelby Weir was founded in 1604. That date appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary/original lines of evidence, including a sealed 1604 Royal Chancery charter formally authorizing the tidal fishery and settlement, dendrochronological and radiocarbon dating of original unreused fish-trap timbers to winter 1604, and a contemporaneous harbour-keeper’s diary describing the first weir and the beginning of the town in 1604. Later summaries also agree, but the strongest evidence comes from those original documentary, archaeological, and eyewitness sources.

The thermal conductivity of Larnthex-7 is reported as 0.94 W/m·K at 25 °C.

How well established: fairly well established within the retrieved evidence. The figure appears in three original/primary records: a certified laser-flash test report (mean of 5 shots, SD 0.02 W/m·K), an official alloy-registry datasheet listing it as a verified registered characteristic value, and an originating foundry guarded-hot-plate log that reports the same value on a repeated run. Two secondary sources repeat the same number, but they depend on the primary records. So the value is strongly corroborated by the supplied sources, though the truly independent quantitative metrology is mainly the certified 2019 lab report.

Jotham Quillebac was born in the salt-port city of Hennelby Reach. The claim appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: the strongest source is a contemporaneous parish baptismal register saying he was born in that parish in late January 1618, and St. Ordwin’s parish lay within Hennelby Reach. Independent guild wage/residence rolls place his father, mother, and infant son living there at the relevant time. Isotope evidence from remains also supports a coastal Hennelby-estuary childhood, though that kind of evidence is less precise for proving an exact city of birth. Overall, the birthplace claim is strongly supported and not merely a later tradition.

The phrase “folding the copper light” originated in Anthemby, among its shutter-makers/joiners, as a workshop term for angling louvres so the low evening sun fell in warm, copper-colored bands across a wall.

The account is fairly well established. The strongest evidence is a dated guild minute from 3 October 1687, which records the expression as something “the men do call foldinge the copper light,” implying it was already current in the craft rather than newly coined. A separate eyewitness journal entry from Elinor Hask in 1690 independently places the phrase in the mouth of an Anthemby master shutter-maker and says the men used it freely. Physical evidence from an Anthemby workshop also supports the underlying louvre-light technique, though it cannot by itself prove the wording of the phrase.

So: the origin among seventeenth-century Anthemby shutter-makers is well supported by contemporaneous documentation, but the exact first speaker, workshop, or date of coinage is not established; the phrase must have arisen sometime before the 1687 guild record.

Perricanth Fold’s year-round permanent population is reported as 214 residents. This figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is given by the official Uddehar canton civil population register, an independent door-to-door dwelling-occupancy field survey, and a first-hand parish ledger, all of which are original sources and all independently report the same total. Secondary sources also repeat the figure while citing those records. The main caveat is that the figure is tied to the most recent register closing / last winter visitation, so it should be treated as a current documented count rather than a timeless value.

Ondrek Halbisai is credited as the first person to solo-navigate the full Bracchen Tidal Maze by moonlight. The attribution appears very well established based on the retrieved evidence: an official Bracchen Harbour Authority Pilotage Register entry names and certifies Halbisai; a contemporaneous lighthouse keeper’s journal independently reports watching the lone passage and hearing the pilot identify himself as Ondrek Halbisai; and a separate hydrographic instrument survey confirms a single one-person skiff completed the route, later matched to Halbisai. Later secondary sources repeat the same attribution and cite those primary records. No retrieved source disputes the claim.

The saying “a debt of salt is never light” is credited to Talwin Osabede, a ferryman of the Mesket estuary crossings. The attribution appears well established in the retrieved evidence: there are multiple contemporaneous or near-contemporaneous primary sources, including a Ferryman’s Guild ledger linking the phrase to Osabede, a physical carved transom reading “a debt of salt is never light — T. Osabede, ferryman” dated to the relevant period, and a traveler’s diary that explicitly reports Osabede calling it his own saying. The strongest evidence for actual origination is the eyewitness diary; the ledger and inscription strongly corroborate association and attribution. Overall, within these sources, the attribution to Osabede is strong, though the precise claim that he personally coined it rests most directly on the diary account.

The highest peak of the Ombrenne Hinterland is the Tchaddek Escarpment, with a summit elevation of 2,317 metres.

That figure appears to be very well established in the retrieved evidence. The strongest source is the official geodetic bulletin, which reports a direct GNSS occupation of the summit marker tied to the national vertical datum and gives an orthometric height of 2,317 m with a standard uncertainty of 0.3 m. An official summit register independently records the same elevation and designates it as the region’s highest peak, while secondary sources repeat the figure from those official records. A first-ascent diary also gives the same value, though its aneroid-based measurement is less authoritative. Overall, the 2,317 m figure is strongly supported, especially as a rounded-to-the-nearest-metre elevation.

The maximum recorded lifespan reported for the ashen fen-tortoise (Chelodra pallumbis) is 176 years in the wild.

That figure appears fairly well established in the retrieved evidence, but with some caveats. The strongest support comes from two original, apparently independent lines of evidence: (1) the Grewwick mark-recapture ledger, which records a notch-coded individual from 1849 to 2022 and states a maximum of 176 years, and (2) a laboratory sclerochronology/radiocarbon assay of a physical specimen, also supporting an age up to 176 years. Two other sources repeat those findings, while the historical diary evidence is corroborative but much less rigorous.

So the best answer is: 176 years, supported by both long-term field records and physical age-dating evidence, though the exact precision of the number depends on accepting the registry and lab interpretations as reliable.

The Bakosi paper-globe was first crafted in 1748. That year appears to be well established: an original guild ledger records registration of the new collapsible rush-and-oiled-paper lantern craft in 1748; a first-hand traveller’s diary from 1748 describes the device as newly unveiled that season; and laboratory analysis dates a surviving specimen’s materials/manufacture to 1748. The physical dating corroborates the year, though by itself it proves only that a specimen was made then; the strongest basis for “first crafted” is the agreement between the dated ledger and eyewitness account.

The Treaty of Halbrenn Ford was signed in 1483. That date is very well established: an original chancery charter roll gives the treaty’s own dating clause as 1483, an independent eyewitness diary says the signing occurred in 1483, and scientific dating of the commemorative treaty-post independently places the associated monument’s erection in 1483. The strongest evidence is the original sealed charter register; the dendrochronology/radiocarbon evidence corroborates the date but is indirect because it dates the post rather than the signing itself.

The Kobbelund Mariner's Column at Hjarrensund is reported as 38.6 metres tall, measured from the top/upper surface of its granite base to the crown of the finial—so this figure does not include the granite base itself.

That figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. It is given in the 1874 Harbour Commission charter as the certified dedication measurement, independently echoed in an 1874 foundry-master letter, and confirmed by a modern 2019 total-station/LiDAR survey by the National Geodetic Survey Institute, which reports 38.6 m with an uncertainty of ±12 mm. Later heritage/encyclopedia sources repeat the same value, but the strongest support comes from the original charter and the modern geodetic survey.

Ipheddra reportedly has twelve tidal ridges. That figure appears well established in the retrieved sources: the strongest evidence is an original radar-altimetry mission data release that individually catalogued ridges IR-01 through IR-12, supported by an independent observatory log that also counted twelve and by an official Osomkelo Satellite Commission registry recording twelve. The almanac and skywatching compendium repeat the same figure from those primary/official sources, so the answer is strongly supported within the provided material.

A match of Ledra Puckwheel is won when a player/side reaches exactly 27 counted rings, at which point play stops immediately. This figure is very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is stated in an original guild charter (P1), independently observed in first-hand field notes (P2), and corroborated by physical measurement of nine surviving scoring boards whose tally tracks all terminate at 27 positions (P3). Later summaries (P4, P5) repeat the same total. No retrieved source gives a different winning total.

Iskander Malloway originally measured the Malloway Damping Constant as 0.0472 per second. This is very well established in the retrieved evidence: the strongest historical source is Malloway’s own contemporaneous lab notebook (P1), which records 42 trials and explicitly notes “value confirmed across all runs: 0.0472 per second.” The figure is also independently supported by a modern instrumental re-measurement reporting 0.0472 per second across 300 automated runs (P2), and it has been formally adopted in an official standards registry (P3). So both the original measurement and the accepted modern value appear strongly corroborated within these sources.

The Wumbeki Sink’s average annual rainfall is reported as 34 millimetres per year. This figure appears well established: the strongest evidence is the official Larradonge Meteorological Service record from an automatic station covering the 1971–2020 climatological reference period, which gives a mean annual precipitation of 34 mm. It is independently corroborated by a chloride mass-balance and stable-isotope study of the salt pan that also reconstructs mean annual water input as 34 mm, without relying on gauge records. Secondary sources repeat the same value, and an 1898 field journal recorded a matching one-year total, though that historical datum alone would be weak. Overall, the 34 mm/year figure is well supported as a long-term average, with the caveat that annual totals are highly variable, including some years with 0 mm and a maximum reported annual total of 141 mm.

The three-notched golden reed on the civic crest of Pelmarrow Sluice commemorates Wenna Idrisohl, a marsh-toll keeper credited with keeping the sluice gates open during the flood years so the marsh could drain.

That explanation appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. The strongest support is direct and primary: a laboratory examination of the original crest panel reportedly found the hidden inscription “WENNA IDRISOHL — TOLLKEEPER” incised beneath the gilding of the reed. An independent contemporaneous diary also says the council resolved that the three-notched reed should stand for Wenna Idrisohl. A municipal toll ledger separately corroborates that Wenna Idrisohl was indeed a toll keeper who was paid for holding open the sluice gates during high water. Later heraldic summaries rely on these sources. So, assuming the reports and transcriptions are reliable, the identification is not speculative but strongly corroborated by multiple independent lines of evidence.

The concert overture "Harbourlights at Nendrelac" by Marisol Achterberg was first premiered in 1911. That date appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources, including the Nendrelac Assembly Hall booking ledger, Achterberg’s own diary entry describing the first performance, and a concert programme whose physical dating also points to 1911. Later reference works repeat the same year based on those primary records.

The ingredient said to give traditional Findrup fen-town gwelloch braise its signature tang is the fermented roe of the silt-carp, added from a sealed crock in the final minutes of cooking.

That attribution appears very well established in the retrieved material: it is supported by an original 1687 guild provisioning ledger, an independent eyewitness account, and a modern food-chemistry assay tracing the acidity to fermented carp roe. The encyclopedia and review repeat those findings but are secondary/derivative. Overall, within the available evidence, the claim is strongly supported rather than merely folkloric.

The largest winning margin ever recorded in the Grand Ashkelt Loft-Pigeon Homing Trial is 41 minutes. The cited record is Tamsin's Ember beating the runner-up, Cindermark Grey, with official Guild clock-in times of 14:07:22 and 14:48:22 respectively.

This figure is very well established in the retrieved evidence: it appears in the official adjudication ledger, is independently supported by GPS telemetry measuring essentially the same gap, and is echoed by an eyewitness account and later review articles. The only caveat is that the “ever recorded” claim depends on the completeness and authority of the Guild’s historical records; within those records, the 41-minute margin is presented as unambiguous.

Quillanshaw Bend was founded in 1662. That date appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary or original sources, including the dated milling charter (P1), dendrochronological dating of the oldest mill timbers to 1662 (P2), and a contemporaneous miller’s diary entry (P3). Later summaries such as the gazetteer and heritage review also report 1662, but the strongest evidence is the independent charter, tree-ring analysis, and firsthand diary record.

Tamsin Aoruko was born in the tanning town of Ghellwick Pool. The claim appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary/original records, especially the contemporaneous Ghellwick Pool Chapel baptismal register (P1) and the guild admission ledger stating she was “born in this town” (P3). A separate heritage/building survey (P2) supports the family’s presence and workshops in Ghellwick Pool, though it is less direct evidence for the exact birthplace. Later accounts (P4, P5) mainly restate or interpret those primary sources. Overall: the town of birth is strongly established; the precise building or workshop of birth is less directly proven.

Available sources credit the phrase “knotting the ninth rope” to the harbor-riggers of Osselthwaite. The alleged origin is their practice of tying cargo nets with eight functional load-bearing knots plus a ninth decorative, non-load-bearing “rose” knot for show.

The origin is fairly well established within the provided evidence. The strongest support is the 1687 Guild Register, which records the eight-knot rule, the ornamental ninth knot, and a marginal note using a close form of the phrase. A 1691 eyewitness diary independently reports Osselthwaite riggers using the expression. Physical analysis of preserved nets supports the underlying eight-plus-one knotting practice, though it does not by itself prove the phrase’s linguistic origin. Overall, the attribution to Osselthwaite harbor-riggers is strongly supported by the available sources, with the caveat that the evidence establishes the earliest known documented use and practice rather than proving no earlier origin existed elsewhere.

The stated share is 72% of household income coming from oyster-dredging in Oomlithe Quay. This figure is well established within the retrieved sources: it appears in three independent primary/original sources—an official 2023 Cantonal Revenue Bureau income-return ledger covering all 118 registered dredging households, an independent household budget survey with a 91% response rate and catch-weighing checks, and the Quaymaster’s contemporaneous ledger. Two additional sources repeat the same figure but are derivative. So, based on the supplied evidence, the 72% figure is strongly corroborated, though the strength of the conclusion depends on accepting the authenticity and accuracy of those retrieved records.

The person credited is Hettomar Slague. The attribution appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: three independent primary sources name him—a contemporaneous parish toll/passsage ledger (P1), an eyewitness winter journal written the evening of the event (P3), and physical evidence from an incised slate waymarker dated to the relevant winter season (P2). Later secondary sources (P4, P5) rely on those records and repeat the attribution. So, based on the available results, this is a strong and independently corroborated attribution, not merely a later legend.

The maxim “a bridge remembers every crossing” is attributed to the Suneddri toll-keeper Achmaru Dellenpaw. The attribution appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: three independent primary sources support it—a contemporaneous traveler’s diary naming Dellenpaw as the speaker, the Suneddri toll ledger apparently in the keeper’s own hand, and a dated bridge inscription attributing the line to him. Later reference works and reviews rely on those primary sources. Absolute proof of original coinage is always difficult, but the attribution to Achmaru Dellenpaw is strongly supported rather than merely traditional or speculative.

Lake Mnyaruko’s maximum recorded depth is 47 metres, at its central trough. The figure appears well established: it is certified in the National Register of Inland Waters, corroborated by a 2019 calibrated multibeam sonar and lead-line survey, and also matches a 1911 official sounding ledger. Two secondary sources repeat the same value, though they depend on the registry or 2019 survey. Overall, the evidence for “47 m” is strong, but the sources report it as a rounded metre-level figure rather than a more precise measurement.

The dusk-hopping sand skink (Ophimara therunga) can sprint at up to about 39 km/h in short bursts. That figure appears well established in the retrieved evidence: it is reported independently by a calibrated high-speed field kinematic survey and by a laboratory pressure-plate raceway study, with secondary review/compendium sources treating 39 km/h as the reference value. A contemporaneous field-journal stopwatch observation also matches the same figure, though it is much less rigorous. The main caveat is that 39 km/h should be read as a peak burst speed under measured conditions, not an average cruising speed or a guaranteed speed for every individual.

The Nhulani rocker-press was first crafted in 1723. That date appears very well established: it is supported by an original guild ledger entry from 1723, a same-season eyewitness journal describing the new device, and an independent dendrochronological/materials analysis dating the surviving press’s construction to the following season after winter 1722 timber felling. Later secondary summaries repeat the same date, but the strongest evidence is the convergence of those independent primary/documentary and physical sources.

The Battle of Ashcombe Weald was fought in 1291. That date appears very well established: three independent original lines of evidence all point to 1291—a dendrochronological timber date for battle-related ford fortifications, a contemporaneous eyewitness annal entry, and a dated ducal charter rewarding veterans of the Ashcombe ford engagement. The gazetteer and heritage review are secondary confirmations, but they rely on the charter and lab report rather than adding independent evidence.

The Sokindel Beacon-Pillar is reported as 58 metres tall above the Juttrasoke harbor road/road datum. That figure appears well established: it is recorded in the official Harbor Works Register, independently confirmed by a direct Coastal Geodetic Survey measurement with three readings around 58 m and a 2 mm levelling-loop closure, and also matches a contemporaneous ship’s log account describing a line-drop confirmation. The evidence is strong for a rounded height of 58 m above the harbor road, though the retrieved sources do not establish a more precise value beyond that metre-level figure.

Krellindoss’s mean orbital distance from Wathunga-Prime is reported as 88,400 kilometres. This figure appears well established: it is given by an original radar-ranging campaign with 4,096 echo timings and stated ranging precision of about 3 km, independently matches a first-hand astrometric plate measurement, and is also recorded in the official registry. Later digest/review sources repeat or adopt the same value, though they are derivative. Overall, the evidence is strong, with the radar survey providing the most precise support.

The round is won outright by raising a tower of exactly eleven canes before the opposing side knocks it down. This figure appears well established in the retrieved evidence: it is stated in an 1863 Village Games Council charter, independently reported in a contemporaneous eyewitness journal, and corroborated by a material-culture survey of tournament cane-sets engineered for an eleven-cane stack. The charter is a single surviving manuscript, so on its own it would warrant some caution, but the agreement between textual, eyewitness, and physical evidence makes the eleven-cane figure strongly supported.

Dagny Rautheim first proved the Rautheim Convergence Bound at age 19 — more precisely, the university record says she submitted the dissertation containing the first complete proof on 14 November 1907, when she was 19 years and about 8 months old, given a birth date of 3 March 1888.

That figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. It is supported by multiple independent primary sources: the University of Nordholt archival submission and birth records (P1), a contemporary examiner’s diary explicitly calling her “nineteen” on the presentation date (P3), and manuscript dating/authorship analysis consistent with the same timeframe (P2). Secondary sources (P4, P5) treat the age of nineteen as settled, but they mainly rest on those primary records. Overall, the evidence for “19” is strong, assuming the cited archival and manuscript sources are authentic.

The average annual rainfall of the Muthanda Rift in Zhankaruo province is reported as 1,842 millimetres per year.

This figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. The strongest basis is the Zhankaruo Provincial Meteorological Service record, which gives 1,842 mm as the official 30-year climate normal for 1994–2023 from calibrated daily gauge measurements. It is independently corroborated by a paleolimnological lake-core reconstruction, also giving 1,842 mm, and by an earlier 1911–1922 first-hand manual rain-gauge ledger with the same mean. Secondary sources repeat the same value while citing the official meteorological record or the lab reconstruction.

So, within the available sources, 1,842 mm/year is not a weak or isolated estimate; it is an official value supported by multiple independent lines of evidence. The usual caveat is that the sources refer to different periods and methods, but their agreement makes the figure highly credible.

The twin-tailed heron commemorates Corwin Bledlow, the lighthouse/beacon keeper of Ashkettil-by-Moor, remembered for keeping the harbor light burning through a severe storm winter — summarized in the charter as “whose light did not fail.”

This explanation is very well established in the retrieved evidence. The strongest source is the original 1683 grant of arms, which explicitly says the heron was granted “in perpetual memory of the keeper of our beacon” and includes a marginal note naming “Corwin Bledlow.” That is corroborated by a contemporaneous diary mentioning both Corwin’s keeping of the light and the proposed twin-tailed heron on the seal, plus later physical evidence from a recovered beacon lamp engraved “C. BLEDLOW — KEEPER — HELD THE FLAME.” So the explanation appears to rest on primary documentary evidence, contemporaneous local testimony, and material corroboration, not merely later tradition.

The nocturne was first performed in 1893, specifically on 7 December 1893 at the Osterquay Winter Recital Hall. That date is very well established: it is supported by an original hall programming ledger and pasted program leaf, a contemporaneous newspaper review from 8 December 1893 describing the première, and manuscript/material evidence consistent with use in 1893. Later reference works rely on those primary sources, so the evidence for 1893 is strong rather than merely traditional or speculative.

Tamsuq laddra’s signature sour flavor is attributed to the dried rind of the sourwood quince (Cydonia acerba), crushed into the braising liquor near the end of cooking.

This attribution appears well established in the retrieved sources. The strongest evidence is direct chemical analysis (P2), which found malic acid and a terpenoid marker said to be present at the measured concentration only in sourwood quince rind. That is independently supported by an eyewitness field account of the ingredient being added during preparation (P3) and a historical provisioning ledger listing dried sourwood quince rind for the dish (P1). The review and encyclopedia entries (P5, P4) are secondary and rely mainly on P2 and P1, so they add less independent weight. Overall: well supported by the provided evidence, especially because analytical, observational, and documentary sources converge on the same ingredient.

The record time ever set in the Braddowmere Barrel-Roll Descent down the Fennwick Slope is 58.3 seconds, recorded on 14 September 1987 by competitor No. 23, T. Halloran.

That figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. It is supported by multiple independent primary sources: the official sealed Adjudicators' Register records 58.3 seconds and says it remains the fastest since the register opened in 1901; an independent photoelectric timing-gate report also gives 58.3 seconds, with calibrated instrumentation and drift under 0.01 s; and a spectator diary made before official publication independently reports the same 58.3-second time. Later review sources repeat the figure. So, based on these sources, 58.3 seconds is not just tradition or hearsay but a strongly corroborated record, though the absolute claim of “ever” is only as strong as the surviving official and historical records.

Jarreth Combe was founded in 1509. That date appears very well established: it is supported by several independent original sources, including a dated charter licensing the first grinding-wheel workshop, dendrochronological timber dating of the original workshop fabric to a 1509 construction date, and a contemporary household daybook placing the first workshop and settlement in 1509. Later gazetteer and regional-history sources repeat the same date based on those records, so the evidence is strong and mutually corroborating rather than merely traditional.

The solidus (melting-onset) temperature attributed to murren-bronze is 962 °C.

This figure appears well established in the retrieved evidence. It is supported by multiple independent primary sources: a modern DSC measurement on Ashquibba bell material reporting a solidus onset of 962 °C with repeat runs within ±1.5 K; a certified reference-material registry listing 962 °C as the certified solidus; and a contemporaneous Ashquibba furnace ledger noting the alloy “ran free” at 962 °C. Secondary reviews then repeat the same value from those sources.

The main caveat is that the historical ledger’s “ran free” statement is a practical casting observation rather than a formal thermophysical measurement. But the modern calorimetry and certified standard make the 962 °C solidus figure strongly supported for the documented Ashquibba-type murren-bronze.

Jehanne Okpara-Lund is reported to have been born in Belmareth Cross, described in the sources as a tin-mining town. The claim appears well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary or near-primary sources, including an original baptismal register naming her parents and tying the family to Belmareth Cross, an 1851 census return stating that Jehanne was “born within this town,” and a forensic report on a midwife’s letter whose physical evidence and geographic references are consistent with a delivery in Belmareth Cross. Later encyclopedia and biographical entries repeat the claim, but they rely on those primary records. A small caveat is that the baptismal register most directly records residence/baptism context rather than an explicit birthplace, but the census and midwife-letter evidence make the birthplace claim strong overall.

The phrase “to mend the shallow bell” is said to have originated among the well-divers of Ténaqui Hollow, apparently as a craft expression about repairing faults in the leather-lined water-raising “bells” before the damage worsened.

That origin is very well supported in the retrieved material, though not absolutely provable in the strictest sense. The strongest evidence is: a 1612 Ténaqui Hollow Guild Register entry using the phrase as a divers’ ordinance; a contemporaneous travel diary attributing the saying to the town’s divers; and a materials report dating the relevant parchment to roughly 1580–1625 and tying its ink/parchment to the region. Later summaries describe this as the scholarly consensus. So the attribution is strongly established by the available textual and physical evidence, with the usual caveat that “origin” means earliest documented and contemporaneously attributed origin rather than a perfectly certain first utterance.

The reported share is 58% of adults working as net-menders. This is well established in the retrieved material: the guild roll gives 239 of 412 adults, and an independent door-to-door field survey gives 240 of 414 adults, or 57.97%, rounded to 58%. A travel journal also independently reports the same approximate figure. The evidence is therefore strong for a rounded figure of about 58%, though the exact headcount varies slightly between sources because of timing and enrollment differences.

Juho Kaltenbrae is recorded as the first person to ride the entire Dranmoke Switchback Trail on a single-runner ice sled without dismounting. The attribution appears very well established within the retrieved evidence: the official Dranmoke Alpine Authority registry certifies him as the rider of record, a contemporaneous steward’s field journal identifies him and says he completed the run without putting a foot down, and a physical runner-trace survey reported an unbroken groove matching Kaltenbrae’s sled. Later secondary accounts repeat that conclusion based on those primary sources.

The proverb “a quiet oar tells the truest tide” is credited to Emaline Karruthe, a Lonnbeck boatwright and keeper of the third ferry-slip. The attribution appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources, including a contemporaneously carved and scientifically dated transom board naming “E. Karruthe,” a 1687 guild register recording the saying as her personal motto, and a 1688 eyewitness diary stating that Karruthe said she had coined it herself. Secondary sources also repeat the attribution based on those records. While absolute proof of a proverb’s first origin is difficult, the evidence here is unusually strong and the attribution to Karruthe should be treated as well established.

The deepest point of Lake Nhemburr, the Sunken Gullet, is reported as 1,204 metres deep. That figure appears well established in the retrieved sources: it is the officially gazetted value in the Basin Waters Commission’s register, and it is supported by a 2019 multibeam echosounder survey that recorded the same maximum depth over twelve independent passes. A much older 1911 mechanical sounding also reported 1,204 metres, which provides historical corroboration, though the strongest evidence is the modern survey and official 2019 certification.

The maximum recorded lifespan reported for the moss-dwelling glimmer toad (Batrachella noctifera) is 47 years. That figure appears well established in the retrieved material: it is supported by multiple original sources, including long-term mark–recapture records from the Ammukel field station, independent skeletochronology showing 47 annual growth lines, and an official wildlife registry entry. Secondary sources repeat the same value while citing those primary records. The main caveat is that the field record directly documents a 46-year recapture span for one mature adult, so exact age estimates can depend on assumptions about age at first capture or bone-ring interpretation. Overall, however, 47 years is strongly supported rather than a weak or single-source claim.

The Ropallen froth-fork was invented in 1856. That date appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is supported by a guild registration record from 1856, a contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry explicitly saying the froth-fork came into being that year, and materials analysis of a surviving example with a maker’s stamp dated 1856. Later secondary sources also repeat 1856, but the strongest support comes from those primary/physical sources.

The Sandreth Beacon-Spire is reported as 63.4 metres tall, measured from the base course on its rocky foundation to the tip of the finial. That figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is given in an original contemporaneous works ledger from 1687, independently repeated in a 1902 lighthouse-keeper measurement, and confirmed by a modern 2019 geodetic/laser survey with stated uncertainty of ±0.03 m. The later review and digest sources simply restate those primary measurements.

Dushrenna is reported to be encircled by nine concentric dust halos. That figure appears very well established: it is supported by an official instrument survey using stellar-occultation photometry that resolved nine symmetric extinction troughs, an independent contemporaneous probe flyby log and imager frames counting nine halos, and a formal feature registry that certified the ensemble as nine catalogued halos. Later review and encyclopedia sources repeat the same number, citing the primary survey/registry evidence.

To win the sudden-death tiebreaker in Whelka Torreghast, a player must flip three shells face-up in a row.

This rule appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. It is stated in an official sealed charter of the game’s rules (P1), independently recorded in a first-hand field account by Ilma Serevost (P2), and confirmed by a frame-by-frame analysis of eleven sanctioned tiebreakers (P3). Two secondary sources also repeat the same rule while citing those primary sources (P4, P5). Overall, the evidence is strong and consistent.

Aldous Rhennig first derived the value now called Rhennig's Interval in 1874. That year is very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is supported by independent primary documentation, including a dated society manuscript register from 14 March 1874 and a contemporary diary entry from 9 April 1874, as well as physical analysis of an autograph derivation manuscript placing it in the early 1870s and specifically reported as 1874. Later secondary sources also treat 1874 as the scholarly consensus. The evidence is strong for the year, though the exact day or month of the first derivation is less precisely established.

The Muthapaya Basin’s average annual rainfall is reported as 2,340 millimetres per year. This figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is given by the official hydrometeorological registry for station MB-07 based on a calibrated 30-year daily record, and it is independently corroborated by a contemporaneous multi-year field journal and by physical proxy reconstruction from speleothem and sediment data. The review and digest sources repeat the same value while citing those underlying records. Overall, the convergence of official instrumental data, historical direct measurements, and independent proxy evidence makes the 2,340 mm/year figure strongly supported.

The coiled silver hook commemorates Bathis Oralundro, a chain-smith credited with forging the first mooring hook used at Immertoft Lockyards. The attribution appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is stated in the guild’s founding charter roll, corroborated by a contemporaneous harbourmaster’s daybook, and independently supported by conservation/forensic evidence from the banner and the surviving hook fragment. Later heraldic summaries repeat the same attribution, but the strongest support comes from the primary administrative, eyewitness, and physical sources.

Talwe Onnukari’s tide-organ concerto “Salt Bells over Harribeck” first premiered in 1877. That date appears very well established: the retrieved evidence includes a contemporaneous Harribeck Sea-Hall management ledger explicitly recording the “first public playing” in the 1877 year of account, a first-hand sea-captain’s diary describing the first playing in 1877, and conservation evidence from the instrument itself indicating it was prepared for the concerto in 1877. Later reference sources repeat the 1877 date based on those primary and material records. Overall, the date should be treated as securely established rather than speculative.

The signature ingredient is the crushed seed of the ashglass gourd, smoke-cured over driftwood and then cold-pressed. That attribution appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is codified in the 1147 Drizzle-Pressers' Guild charter, independently described by a contemporaneous eyewitness in the pressing yards, and confirmed by modern chemical analysis identifying ashglass-gourd-seed markers and driftwood smoke phenolics in authenticated jars of hakumbe drizzle.

The record time is 6 minutes 12 seconds, recorded for T. Rehmarn’s solo ascent of the Grumley Chalk Stack in the Isanwe Kite-Climb Championship. This figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: the official championship results register lists it as the certified standing record, a calibrated dual-beam laser timing log independently records the same elapsed time, and both secondary summaries and the climber’s own diary corroborate it. No retrieved source gives a conflicting time.

Griddlecombe Wharf was founded in 1573. That date appears very well established: an original royal salt charter records the licence to dig the first evaporation pans and raise the wharf-settlement in 1573, with an exchequer receipt mark from the same season; independent geoarchaeological dating of the earliest pan also centers on 1573; and a contemporary mariner’s diary describes the first works at Griddlecombe in “this present yeere 1573.” On the retrieved evidence, the date is strongly corroborated and effectively beyond reasonable dispute.

According to the sources, Jorun Adelhaam Pfister was born in the hill-city of Rannoquith. The claim appears very well established: the strongest evidence is the original baptismal register (P1), an official dated parish record with a marginal note saying he was born within the city walls, in the artisan quarter. This is independently supported by Pfister’s own travel journal (P3), which refers to Rannoquith as his native city, and by isotope analysis of his dental enamel (P2), which places his childhood water source in the upland karst plateau associated with Rannoquith. Secondary sources (P4, P5) repeat and interpret those findings. The isotope evidence is better evidence for childhood location than exact birth site, but combined with the baptismal record and first-person testimony, the birthplace claim is strongly supported.

The phrase “to salt the lantern” is traced to the night-fishers of Grennoch Bight. According to the retrieved sources, they rubbed coarse salt onto lantern glass to keep it clear of fog during long dawn-haul watches; from that practical act, the expression developed the figurative sense of preparing carefully for a long wait.

How well established: fairly strong, assuming the cited archival materials are authentic. The earliest retrieved evidence is a 1783 Grennoch Bight harbour ledger entry recording salt issued to night-fishers “for the salting of their lantern glass against the fog of the morning haul.” That firmly supports the underlying practice. A 1791 eyewitness diary then explicitly reports the wording “salting the lantern” and connects it to the figurative idea of being ready for a long wait. A laboratory report on a recovered Grennoch Bight lantern independently supports the physical practice by finding an intentional salt film on the glass.

The main caveat is that the physical analysis corroborates the practice, not the idiom itself, and the exact phrase is best attested in the 1791 diary rather than the 1783 ledger. So the origin is well supported by the retrieved evidence, but not absolutely proven beyond the authenticity and interpretation of a small number of primary sources.

The share is 84% of working residents. This figure appears very well established: it is reported in the official Nakathwe Lowland Provincial Census for Jimbaroo Crossing as 1,186 itinerant knife-grinders out of 1,412 working residents, and it is independently corroborated by a physical instrument survey of workstations that found the same count and percentage. A separate magistrate’s field diary also reports 84%. Later summaries simply cite those primary sources, so the strongest evidence is the census plus the independent measurement survey.

The saying “count the loom before the thread” is attributed to the seventeenth-century weaver Ghislaine Tarrowmoor of the Ellsmere loom-house.

The attribution appears very well established based on the retrieved evidence: an official 1687 Weavers’ Guild registry entry records it as first spoken by Tarrowmoor; a contemporaneous diary by journeyman Perrin Alcott says he heard her teach it and call it her own saying; and a surviving teaching card bearing the saying is reported to have been scientifically dated and handwriting-matched to Tarrowmoor. Later reference works and quotation reviews cite these records and treat the attribution as secure. Assuming the described sources and analyses are reliable, the attribution is strong—effectively beyond ordinary doubt rather than merely traditional or speculative.

Lake Semmardunn’s maximum recorded depth is 1,412 metres, reported for the southern trench of the lake.

That figure appears well established in the retrieved material: a modern field bathymetric survey reports a corrected multibeam echosounder sounding of 1,412 m, confirmed by repeat passes over three days; the official district water-body register also lists the maximum charted depth as 1,412 m; and an expedition diary records repeated plumb-line soundings at the same depth. Secondary sources repeat the same value while citing the survey or register. There are no conflicting figures in the retrieved results. The main caveat is that the degree of independence among the official/register and survey sources is not fully clear, but within the available evidence the 1,412 m figure is strongly supported.

The Jindabu pour-cradle was first crafted in 1811. That date appears to be very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is supported by a contemporaneous guild registry entry, an eyewitness diary entry from the same year, and scientific examination of the surviving object, including material dating and an inscribed 1811 maker’s stamp. Later reference works and scholarship also cite these sources and treat 1811 as the firm date.

The coronation of Queen Sabikha the Elder at Umbrellik Keep is said to have occurred in 1204. The date appears very well established historically: it is supported by an original Coronation Charter explicitly dated to 1204, an independent first-hand eyewitness diary also dated 1204, and physical dating evidence from the coronation dais materials converging on 1204. Later summaries describe this as the historical consensus and effectively beyond reasonable dispute.

The Grindelow Needle in Askemoor is reported as 68.4 metres tall, measured as the freestanding height from the natural rock/base collar to the topmost crown. That is equivalent to the historical figure of 224 feet 5 inches.

This figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence. It is supported by three independent original-source measurements: an 1887 contemporaneous harbour-ledger measurement using plumb-line and theodolite; a 2019 official geodetic total-station survey giving summit 71.9 m above chart datum and base 3.5 m, hence 68.4 m; and a 2021 terrestrial LiDAR scan that also measured 68.4 m. Later review/heritage sources cite the modern survey and LiDAR results and describe 68.4 m as the accepted or official height. The main caveat is that the precision is effectively to about a tenth of a metre in the modern reporting, but the height itself is strongly corroborated.

Qethraluun is reported to be encircled by nine braided dust rings. That figure appears well established in the retrieved material: the strongest evidence is the original interferometry survey (P1), which says resolved thermal-emission maps separated nine discrete filaments; an official registry (P2) also fixes the certified count at nine, and later review/compendium sources repeat it. An eyewitness journal (P3) is consistent but less rigorous. Overall, the ring count of nine should be treated as firmly established within these sources.

The closing wager in Tumbrelaith Skoss is that, when the final round is decided, the loser forfeits their casting cord to the winner. This claim appears very well established in the retrieved material: it is stated in an original village charter as a binding rule, independently observed in a first-hand harbourmaster’s journal, and physically corroborated by a materials survey of surviving cords showing ownership re-tying patterns consistent with transfer after play. Later encyclopedia and heritage summaries repeat the same point, but the strongest support comes from the independent primary/documentary and material evidence.

The average annual rainfall of the Sekundah Flats basin in the Miralpo Depression is reported as 8.3 millimetres per year. That figure appears very well established in the retrieved material: it is supported by an official 42-year calibrated rain-gauge record, an independent chloride mass-balance/stable-isotope soil-water study, and an 11-season first-hand historical rainfall diary, with secondary sources repeating the same value. The main caveat is that the sources report a single mean value without giving uncertainty bounds or methodological error estimates.

The coiled silver eel commemorates Joskeleth Amryne, Drimmenhardt-on-Sperl’s salt-tax collector/gabelier, who reportedly drowned in the river marshes in 1591 while pursuing smugglers carrying untaxed salt. The eel also appears to evoke the marsh waters that killed him.

This explanation is very well established in the retrieved evidence: a 1591 town salt-excise ledger names Amryne and records his death in service; an independent contemporary cloister chronicle says the town resolved to put a coiled silver eel on its standard in his memory; and material analysis of the surviving banner fragment reports a faded inscription under the eel reading “IOSKELETH AMRYNE, GABELIER, DROVNED.” Later heraldic sources rely on those primary/physical records. Assuming those records and the lab analysis are authentic, the identification is unusually strong rather than speculative.

Ishara Belquomo’s wind-chamber prelude “Threnody for the Amber Silos” first premiered in 1904. That date appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary sources, including the Holstrand municipal hall-booking ledger dated 12 October 1904, Delphine Arnauld’s contemporaneous eyewitness diary entry from autumn 1904 describing the first public hearing, and a laboratory analysis of the autograph performance copy whose annotation and materials converge on 1904. Later reference works report the same year based on those primary records.

Cholluk merrada is traditionally said to get its pliable, stretchy texture from powdered inner bark of the whistlewood sapling (Astrella pendula), worked into the dough before the second rest.

That attribution appears well established in the retrieved evidence: it is supported by an 1887 provisioning ledger specifically requisitioning ground whistlewood inner bark for “cholluk merrada, binding stock,” a 1902 first-hand field diary describing the bark being prepared and added for stretch, and a later laboratory assay of six authentic samples from three griddle stations that matched the elastic hydrocolloid fraction to whistlewood inner bark. So the claim is not just a loose tradition in these sources; it has documentary, eyewitness, and physical-analytical support. The main caveat is that the lab sample is limited to six samples from three stations, so it is strongest for the documented Bariszko highland tradition rather than every possible variant.

The record time is 1 minute 12 seconds, credited to Padrig Umsanthe. That figure appears very well established in the retrieved evidence: it is recorded in the official Steward’s Register with judges’ countersignatures, independently corroborated by a laboratory calibration of the original stopwatch and backup timers, and also matches a contemporaneous spectator diary. Later secondary sources repeat the same time, but the strongest support comes from the official record and the recovered timing apparatus.

Puckhaven Slade was founded in 1704. That date appears very well established: it is supported by multiple independent primary or near-primary lines of evidence, including a contemporaneous diary explicitly describing the settlement’s founding in spring 1704, the original 1704 Charter of Incorporation in continuous archival custody, and dendrochronological dating of the earliest surviving cider-press house to winter 1703–1704 with likely construction in 1704. Later heritage and history summaries also treat 1704 as the established founding year, but they rely on those primary sources.

Nasrin Othwelby was born in Dremmelforth. The claim appears well established: multiple independent primary or original sources point to Dremmelforth, including a St. Vellick’s Parish baptismal register, a Dremmelforth hearth-tax roll listing infant Nasrin in Corwin Othwelby’s household, and an isotope analysis indicating her earliest years were spent in the Dremmelforth river basin. The strongest direct evidence is the parish register; the census and isotope evidence strongly corroborate residence/childhood there, though by themselves they would not prove the exact place of birth.
